tier_reason: README godbolt table (BM_jea 10.2ns vs BM_fmt 16.6ns) is disclaimed by the author as a debug-built Google Benchmark, so it is capped at C. The README also embeds a release win64 VC2019 chart, made with the author's fork of miloyip/itoa-benchmark (src/sprintf.cpp, src/vc.cpp), that compares against sprintf and MSVC _ui64toa. That run states no hardware and no flags, so it is still not A.

corrections.baseline: sprintf (C standard library, MSVC CRT) and MSVC _itoa/_ui64toa in the README's release charts; {fmt} in the godbolt table. No std::to_chars comparison exists.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README godbolt table (debug-built Google Benchmark): BM_jea 10.2ns vs BM_fmt 16.6ns (~1.6x). README-embedded release win64 VC2019 chart (data in docs/release_win64_vc2019.js, y-axis 'cycle count'), uniform-random-length column: u32toa jeaiii::to_text 20.5 vs sprintf 160.5 (~7.8x), vc/_ui64toa 174.5 (~8.5x), fmt 33.5 (~1.6x); u64toa 32.75 vs sprintf 226.75 (~6.9x), vc 312 (~9.5x), fmt 58 (~1.8x). The README also says the latest version is '25% faster' than before.
corrections.workload: u32toa/u64toa conversion of integers with 1..10 (u32) or 1..20 (u64) digits plus a uniform-random-digit-length case. Measured with the author's fork of miloyip/itoa-benchmark (jeaiii/itoa-benchmark), release win64 VC2019, against sprintf, MSVC _ui64toa, {fmt} and other itoa variants. There is also a debug-built Google Benchmark on godbolt vs {fmt}.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Release win64 Visual C++ 2019 for the chart data (exact flags not stated on the page). The godbolt {fmt} comparison used Google Benchmark compiled in debug.
corrections.caveats: The in-repo godbolt comparison vs {fmt} is disclaimed by the author (Google Benchmark compiled in debug). The README says the release VC2019 charts are 'much more accurate'. Those charts compare against sprintf and MSVC _ui64toa (C runtime) but not std::to_chars. They are author-run, with hardware and flags unstated. The src/to_chars.cpp in the benchmark fork is jeaiii's own to_chars implementation, not std::to_chars.

notes: Baseline was a guess (std::to_chars). The README chart actually shows a win vs sprintf/MSVC _ui64toa, roughly 7-9x on random-length inputs, and ~1.6-1.8x vs {fmt}. baseline_stdlib is set to MSVC because the run is VC2019 win64, but sprintf/_ui64toa come from the MSVC C runtime (UCRT), not the STL headers proper. Metadata checked: MIT, 254 stars, last commit 2022-11-24, not a fork, not archived. [orchestrator: baseline_in_list=false, baseline outside category list]

tier_reason: results/btree_benchmark_results.md compares directly against std::map (map_8_32, map_8_256) using in-repo code src/binary/btree_benchmark.cpp and scripts/interleaved_btree_benchmark.py. It states the hardware (Ryzen 9 5950X, isolated core, Linux 6.16.3) and compiler (Clang Release), and CMakeLists.txt pins the Release flags.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang, CMake Release build. CMakeLists.txt (at HEAD) sets -O3 -march=haswell -mtune=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops -fno-trapping-math plus ThinLTO (-flto=thin) and -mavx2 -mfma. Clang version not stated.

notes: All claimed numbers match the page. 10M-element ratios vs std::map range from ~2.1x (ERASE P99.9, 32B) to ~4.8x (INSERT P99.9, 256B). The top config uses the hugepage allocator. At 10K elements with 256B values, std::map wins ERASE P99.9 (213.6 vs 245.7 ns). The README confirms that development was AI-assisted (Claude) and that the project is a work in progress. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 75 stars, last commit 2026-01-06.

tier_reason: The article compares the S+ tree against std::lower_bound, std::set and absl::btree. The linked repo has runnable baselines: binsearch/std.cc (std::lower_bound), binsearch/set.cc (std::multiset), binsearch/bplus.cc and standalone.cc. binsearch/Makefile gives clang++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native, and the article states Clang 10 on a Zen 2 CPU (the CPU model is not named).

corrections.baseline: std::lower_bound (primary), std::set (bench code binsearch/set.cc actually uses std::multiset), absl::btree
corrections.claimed_speedup: Reciprocal throughput. The S+ tree is up to 15x faster than std::lower_bound; the S-tree variant is up to 8x (article). The repo README says ~15x over std::lower_bound for small cache-resident arrays and ~8x for large arrays (>1e6). The S+ tree is up to 30x faster than std::set on the same lower-bound queries, and the S+ tree with pointers is ~15x faster than Abseil's B-tree for large arrays (article). The article says the real-latency speedup is 'not that impressive'.

notes: Numbers verified on the article and the repo README. The record's Abseil wording was garbled: it is the S+ tree with pointers that is ~15x faster than the Abseil B-tree, not an Abseil B-tree 'with pointers'. The last commit on main (the only branch) is 2022-10-06; pushed_at 2022-12-11 is not a commit date. No LICENSE file (GitHub license null), so 'reference' usability is correct. 841 stars.

tier_reason: Upgraded from B, because B needs peer review or an independent third-party suite and this is the author's own benchmark. The speedtest page states compiler, flags and hardware for each run, and the benchmark code is public: bingmann/stx-btree speedtest/speedtest.cc, and its current form in tlx at tests/container/btree_speedtest.cpp. That code runs against libstdc++ std::multiset/std::multimap.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 2007 run: for n > 1,024,000 items, the red-black tree (libstdc++ multiset) needs almost twice as much time as a B+ tree with 32 slots. Per-item insertion diverges beyond ~16,000 items. 2011 run: same qualitative win, with the insertion curves diverging at ~100,000 items. 2013 run: results 'very similar' to 2011, and std::map is noted as much slower than std::set while the B+ tree map is only slightly slower than the B+ tree set. The in-repo tlx results PDF (tests/container/btree_speedtest_results.pdf, 2019) plots tlx::btree_multiset below std::multiset for insert, find and insert/find/delete at large n, roughly 3x at 2^26 items by visual chart reading.
corrections.workload: Random-integer multiset (and, in 2013, map/multimap) tests: insert-only, insert+find+erase, and find-only on pre-filled trees. n runs from 125 to 4,096,000, 32,768,000 or 65,536,000 depending on the run, doubling each step. Several B+ tree slot sizes (4-256) are tested against the libstdc++ red-black tree and hash tables.
corrections.caveats: The page's numbers are 12-19 years old, from Pentium 4 and Core i7 9xx machines with gcc 4.x. The speedtest page belongs to the predecessor stx-btree project (marked OBSOLETE and folded into tlx). tlx does ship its own btree_speedtest.cpp and a 2019 results PDF showing the same win vs std::multiset, but that PDF states no hardware or compiler. The page's speedups are shown mainly as plots, and the text states only the ~2x figure.

notes: The 2013 flags were '-O3 -march=native', not -fomit-frame-pointer plus -march=native. The tier was re-derived as A because both the code and full methodology are public (it is the author's benchmark, not third-party). Metadata checked: BSL-1.0, 458 stars, last commit 2025-01-10 (stale). The predecessor bingmann/stx-btree is GPL-3.0, while the tlx code is BSL-1.0.

tier_reason: A 2014 single-author blog post gives a timing table for boost::container::flat_set vs std::set, with Rcpp benchmark code inline and -O3 stated. The compiler, its version, the hardware and the Boost version (via the R BH package) are not stated, so it is not A, and it is neither peer-reviewed nor a third-party suite.
notes: The table matches the claim. flat_set is 2.51x faster at size 2, ~1.10x at 128, and slower from 256 up, with std::set ~13.4x faster at 8192. The loop is 500,000 random inserts, each followed by an erase only if the insert succeeded, timed with std::clock. Metadata checked: BSL-1.0, 127 stars, last commit 2026-09-23 (active).
